paper_context.research_question: How do two classes of dataset-level metrics—prerequisite skills (types/number of comprehension and reasoning skills required) and readability (lexical/syntactic difficulty)—characterize existing reading comprehension (RC) datasets, and how (if at all) do these two dimensions correlate with one another and with question difficulty?
contribution_style: empirical evaluation across multiple existing datasets
manual annotation and release of labeled subset/results
main_claims: A refined set of thirteen prerequisite skills for RC (derived from prior work and cognitive theories) can be used to annotate questions and characterize question difficulty.
Readability metrics (lexical/syntactic /traditional indices) and the number/types of prerequisite skills capture different aspects of dataset difficulty.

There is only a weak correlation between readability of contexts and the number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions: texts that are easy to read can yield difficult questions and vice versa.

Different existing RC datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space of readability and prerequisite-skill difficulty (e.g., QA4MRE: hard-to-read and hard-to-answer; MCTest: easy-to-read but often hard-to-answer; SQuAD: hard-to-read but relatively easy-to-answer).

Manual annotation of 100 examples per dataset (six datasets) produced high inter-annotator agreement (reported 90.1% on a random subset), and the resulting labels can guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Validity and clarity of the refined prerequisite-skills taxonomy (completeness, mutual exclusivity, theoretical grounding in entailment and cognitive models)
Reliability of annotation (inter-annotator agreement, annotation instructions and edge cases like 'nonsense' or 'no answer')
Representativeness and sampling (100 questions per dataset: sufficiency and sampling method) and potential sampling bias
Appropriateness and choice of readability features (selection from Vajjala & Meurers 2012 and how applied only to sentences marked as necessary)
Statistical analysis of correlation between skills-count and readability (strength, significance, dataset-specific variation)
Generalizability of findings to other RC datasets and task formulations (e.g., cloze, anonymized data excluded)
Utility of annotations for downstream applications (e.g., curriculum learning, dataset construction, system diagnosis)
Limitations acknowledged by authors (cannot evaluate sentence-selection competence; handling of 'none of the above' or externally answerable questions)

extracted_claims.claim_text: A refined set of thirteen prerequisite skills for reading comprehension (RC), reorganized from prior work and cognitive theories, can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: "By refining Sugawara et al. (2017)’s ten reading comprehension skills, we reorganized thirteen prerequisite skills in total..." (Sec. 3.1)

List of 13 skills (Object tracking, Mathematical reasoning, Coreference resolution, Logical reasoning, Analogy, Causal relation, Spatiotemporal relation, Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration, Meta-knowledge, Schematic clause relation, Punctuation).
uncertainty_flags: Authors claim reorganization but provide limited formal validation of taxonomy completeness or mutual exclusivity.
Operational definitions for some skills (e.g., meta-knowledge, bridging vs elaboration) may overlap; boundary cases not exhaustively specified in text.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical/syntactic/traditional indices) and the number/types of prerequisite skills capture different aspects of dataset difficulty (reading ease vs comprehension/ reasoning requirements).
evidence: "Based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)’s depiction of text comprehension, we adopted two classes for the evaluation of RC datasets: prerequisite skills and readability." (Sec. 3)
"To classify these metrics, we can place three classes: lexical features..., syntactic features..., and traditional features (Coleman)." (Sec. 3.2)
uncertainty_flags: Paper assumes the two metric classes are separable; empirical evidence for separability is claimed in later analysis but may depend on metric choice and annotation procedure.
Readability metrics chosen were developed for human readers; applicability to system difficulty is acknowledged as uncertain.

extracted_claims.claim_text: There is only a weak correlation between readability of contexts and the number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions: texts that are easy to read can yield difficult questions and vice versa.
evidence: "Table 5 presents Pearson’s correlation coefficients... Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values." (Sec. 5(iv))
Figures 3 and 4: plots of Flesch–Kincaid grade levels vs average/individual numbers of required skills showing separate dataset domains.
uncertainty_flags: Exact values for Table 5 not reproduced in-text here; strength and statistical significance per dataset and per metric need inspection.
Correlation range (0.025–0.416) includes very small values; the practical significance and p-values are not provided in the quoted text.
Readability measured on sentences selected by annotators (see Sec. 3.2); dependency between sentence selection and skill labels could influence correlations.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Different existing RC datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space of readability and prerequisite-skill difficulty (examples: QA4MRE: hard-to-read & hard-to-answer; MCTest: easy-to-read but often hard-to-answer; SQuAD: hard-to-read but relatively easy-to-answer).
evidence: "QA4MRE was relatively difficult both to read and to answer, and SQuAD was difficult to read but easy to answer." (Sec. 5(iv))
"MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer." (Sec. 5 summary)
uncertainty_flags: Characterization is based on the sampled 100 questions per dataset and the chosen readability and skill metrics; representativeness of samples and metric sensitivity could affect region assignment.
Quantitative boundaries of regions are not formally defined; observations are descriptive.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Manual annotation of 100 examples per dataset (six datasets) produced high inter-annotator agreement (reported 90.1% on a 62-question random subset), and the resulting labels are released to guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.
evidence: "We asked three annotators..." (Sec. 4.1)
"The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions." (Sec. 5)
uncertainty_flags: Agreement reported as a single percentage; the measure used (percent agreement vs. Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) is not specified.
Agreement computed on a 62-question subset (not the full 600); potential variability across datasets or skill labels not reported.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Annotation procedure: annotators saw context, question, and answer jointly, selected sentences needed to answer, and labeled required prerequisite skills; readability metrics were computed only on the selected sentences.
evidence: "The annotators then selected sentences that needed to be read to answer the question and decided if each prerequisite skill was required." (Sec. 4.1)
"We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions." (Sec. 3.2)
uncertainty_flags: Procedure intentionally excludes evaluation of sentence-selection competence; this operational choice links readability measures to annotator-selected subsets rather than whole contexts, possibly biasing readability estimations.
Inter-annotator variability in sentence selection is not reported; may affect downstream metrics.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Dataset-level observations: QA4MRE highest in required skills and readability; MS MARCO relatively easy (many questions with <3 skills) but contains 'nonsense' questions; Who-did-What often requires ellipsis/bridging/elaboration due to its sourcing; NewsQA provides meta-information allowing filtering of nonsense.
evidence: Table 2 and Table 3 frequency summaries (skill frequencies and number-of-skills distributions).
Textual summaries: "QA4MRE had the highest scores...", "MS MARCO and Who-did-What received relatively high scores [for nonsense]...", "NewsQA had no nonsense questions..." (Sec. 5)
uncertainty_flags: Sampling method: 100 randomly selected questions per dataset from specific splits (development or gold-standard) may not capture full dataset distributions.
Definitions and detection of 'nonsense' depend on annotator judgments; variability and thresholds not fully specified.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The two metric classes (readability and prerequisite skills) can guide curriculum-style dataset creation and system development steps: start with easy-to-read/easy-to-answer, progress to easy-to-read/hard-to-answer, then hard-to-read/hard-to-answer.
evidence: "One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset...appropriate datasets can be prepared for every step by measuring their properties using the metrics of this study." (Sec. 6)
uncertainty_flags: Claim is prescriptive and conceptual; empirical validation that following this curriculum improves system learning is not provided in this paper.
Effectiveness may depend on metric reliability and dataset representativeness.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The number of prerequisite skills required to answer a question corresponds to the question's difficulty.
supporting_evidence: "From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question." (Sec. 1)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If skill-count does not reliably map to difficulty (for humans or systems), conclusions about dataset difficulty and comparisons across datasets may be invalid or misleading.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Prerequisite skills taxonomy (13 skills) sufficiently covers the reasoning and comprehension phenomena needed for RC dataset analysis.
supporting_evidence: Authors present taxonomy and state it was reorganized from prior work and theory.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Missing or mis-specified skills would bias annotations, underestimate certain difficulty types, and reduce the taxonomy's utility for dataset construction or system diagnosis.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Readability metrics drawn from Vajjala & Meurers (2012) (top ten features) meaningfully represent 'reading difficulty' relevant to RC tasks when applied to annotator-selected sentences.
supporting_evidence: "We used the classification of linguistic features proposed by Vajjala and Meurers (2012)... We list the readability metrics in Figure 2..."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If metrics do not capture aspects relevant to answering RC questions (especially for automated systems), correlations and dataset characterizations based on these metrics may be misleading.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Annotators can reliably identify the minimal set of sentences 'needed' to answer a question and consistently label required prerequisite skills based on the provided instructions.
supporting_evidence: "The annotators then selected sentences that needed to be read to answer the question and decided if each prerequisite skill was required."
Reported inter-annotator agreement 90.1% on 62 sampled questions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Inconsistent sentence selection or skill labeling would contaminate readability calculations (applied to selected sentences) and skill-frequency statistics, reducing internal validity.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Sampling 100 randomly selected questions per dataset (from development/gold splits as specified) is sufficient to characterize dataset-level properties for analysis and comparison.
supporting_evidence: "We randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset... This amount of questions was considered to be sufficient for the analysis of RC datasets as performed by Chen et al. (2016)."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If 100 samples are not representative (due to dataset heterogeneity, topic distribution, or sampling method), results about frequency distributions, averages, and correlations may not generalize to the full datasets.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Percent agreement (90.1%) is an adequate indicator of annotation reliability for multi-label skill annotations.
supporting_evidence: Reported single agreement figure without specification of metric type.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Percent agreement can be inflated for skewed labels; without chance-corrected measures (e.g., kappa), reliability may be overestimated, especially for multi-label annotations.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Applying readability metrics only to sentences annotators selected captures the reading difficulty relevant to answering the question (rather than analyzing whole-context readability).
supporting_evidence: "We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If necessary reading spans broader context or requires search/selection competence, measuring only selected sentences may under- or over-estimate true reading difficulty for the QA task.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Pearson correlation between number-of-skills and readability metrics is an appropriate statistic to capture relationship between these dimensions.
supporting_evidence: Use of Pearson’s correlation coefficients reported in Table 5 and discussion of weak correlations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the relationship is non-linear or driven by heterogeneous subgroups, Pearson correlation could understate or misrepresent association patterns; significance levels and effect sizes must be examined.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Excluding some datasets (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA) for stated reasons yields a representative selection of RC datasets for the study’s research question.
supporting_evidence: Authors explain exclusions: anonymization, task formulation mismatch, formatting for machine reading.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Exclusions might bias conclusions; omitted dataset types (e.g., cloze/anonymized) could occupy different regions in the metric space, affecting generalizability.

argument_focus: Operationalizing RC difficulty along two orthogonal axes: prerequisite skills (cognitive/entailment-based) and readability (lexical/syntactic).
Empirical characterization of six RC datasets using these metrics and examining correlations and dataset-specific profiles.
Practical utility: annotations as resources to guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.
contribution_targets: Presentation and reorganization of a 13-item prerequisite-skills taxonomy grounded in textual entailment and cognitive models (Sec. 3.1).
An annotation dataset: 100 annotated questions × 6 RC datasets with sentence-selection and multi-label skill annotations (Sec. 4).
Comparative empirical analysis showing weak overall correlation between readability and required skills and describing per-dataset profiles (Sec. 5).
evaluation_targets: Validity and clarity of the 13-skill taxonomy: coverage, mutual exclusivity, operational definitions, and edge cases (Sec. 3.1).
Annotation reliability: choice of agreement metric, per-skill agreement, sentence-selection consistency, and disagreement cases (Sec. 4.1, Sec. 5).
Sampling representativeness: sampling method details per dataset, dependence on chosen splits, and sample size sufficiency (Sec. 4.2, Appendix A).
Readability measurement choices: applying human-focused metrics to annotator-selected sentences, metric preprocessing, and alternative/robustness checks (Sec. 3.2).
Statistical analysis: full reporting of correlation coefficients, p-values, effect sizes, checks for nonlinearity or dataset-specific patterns (Sec. 5(iv)).
Handling of 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' questions: annotation guidelines, prevalence, and impact on analyses (Sec. 4.1, Sec. 5).
uncertainty_flags: Taxonomy boundaries and potential overlap between skills (bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge vs elaboration) are not exhaustively defined.
Inter-annotator agreement reported as a single percent on a subset; lack of chance-corrected reliability measures and per-label agreement statistics.
Readability metrics applied only to annotator-selected sentences — selection variability could confound readability–skill relationships.
Correlation analyses report weak coefficients but do not include p-values or controls for dataset heterogeneity or nonlinearity.
Sampling 100 questions per dataset may be insufficient for datasets with high internal heterogeneity; selection methods vary across datasets (see Appendix A).
'Nonsense' and 'no-answer' cases are acknowledged but treatment and impacts are not fully quantified.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should verify operational definitions for each of the 13 skills and request annotation guidelines and examples used to train annotators (Sec. 3.1, 4.1).
Request full annotation data and per-skill label distributions, confusion matrices, and per-skill inter-annotator agreement (not just overall percent) to assess reliability.
Recompute readability metrics on whole contexts as a sensitivity check (since current approach uses annotator-selected sentences) and test whether results change.
Inspect Table 5 and raw correlations: obtain exact Pearson coefficients, p-values, and consider Spearman or non-parametric tests and dataset-stratified analyses.
Examine sampling code/seed and selection procedure in Appendix A to assess representativeness; check whether sampling produced topic or length skews across datasets.
Clarify how 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' annotations were operationalized and measure their prevalence per dataset; test analyses with and without those items.
Test alternative operationalizations of 'difficulty' (e.g., human response time, existing system performance) and compare correlations with skill-count and readability.
Request release of annotation interface and instruction text to evaluate annotator cues (especially for sentence selection and 'nonsense' judgments).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that reading-comprehension (RC) dataset difficulty is usefully decomposed into two largely distinct axes: prerequisite skills (a refined 13-item taxonomy operationalized via multi-label annotations) and readability (a set of lexical/syntactic features). The paper operationalizes both axes, annotates six RC datasets (100 examples each) with sentence-selection and skill labels, computes readability on annotator-selected sentences, and reports descriptive statistics and Pearson correlations. The central empirical claim is that readability and required prerequisite skills are weakly correlated, and that datasets occupy different regions in the joint space. The paper provides a resource (annotations) and proposes that these metrics can guide dataset design and curriculum-style system development. The main logical chain is: (1) cognitive theory motivates two evaluation classes; (2) refine/define a skills taxonomy; (3) collect annotations with sentence-selection and skill labels; (4) compute readability on selected sentences; (5) compare datasets and compute correlations; (6) interpret weak correlations to motivate dataset construction/use. Strengths include clear operationalization and multi-dataset empirical work; main weaknesses are potential circularities/measurement dependencies (readability measured on annotator-selected sentences), limited reporting of annotation reliability/statistics (single percent agreement on a subset, no kappa or per-skill agreement), sampling representativeness (100 items/dataset), and limited statistical rigor (Pearson coefficients reported but p-values, effect sizes, robustness checks, or nonparametric tests not shown). Several assumptions undergird the conclusions (notably that skill-count maps to difficulty and that skill taxonomy is sufficiently complete and distinct).
logical_argument_graph: Node A: RC difficulty is multi-dimensional; reading ease and comprehension/reasoning are distinct (motivated by McNamara & Magliano 2009).
Node B: Prior work (Sugawara et al.) showed skill-count relates to difficulty but had limited scope; therefore taxonomy refinement is needed.
Edge A->B: Theoretical motivation justifies refining prerequisite skills and pairing with readability metrics.
Node C: Define/refine 13 prerequisite skills grounded in textual entailment and cognitive models (Kintsch, McNamara).
Node D: Define readability metrics (top features from Vajjala & Meurers) and apply to sentences.
Edge C+D->E: Operationalize both axes to permit dataset-level measurement.
Node E: Annotation procedure: 3 annotators, select needed sentences and multi-label skills for 100 examples per dataset.
Node F: Compute dataset-level statistics: skill frequencies, #skills distribution, readability scores, sentence counts/distances.
Edge E->F: Annotation outputs feed descriptive measures.
Node G: Compute correlations (Pearson) between #skills and readability metrics; visualize joint space (Figures 3–4).
Edge F->G: Use computed measures to test relationship hypothesis.
Node H: Empirical conclusion: readability and prerequisite-skill difficulty are weakly correlated; datasets occupy distinct regions.
Edge G->H: Observed weak Pearson coefficients and plotted clusters support conclusion.
Node I: Practical claim: metrics can inform dataset construction and curriculum learning.
Edge H->I: If axes are distinct and reliably measurable, they can drive curriculum ordering.

Break/Weak Link 1: Readability computed only on annotator-selected sentences (E->D link) introduces measurement dependence and possible circularity: annotator skill labels determine which sentences are measured, so readability and skill-count may be entangled via annotator behavior.

Break/Weak Link 2: Reliability of annotations insufficiently quantified (E node weak): single percent agreement on subset, no chance-corrected stats or per-skill agreement undermines confidence in F and downstream G/H.
Break/Weak Link 3: Statistical inference limited (G node weak): Pearson coefficients reported without p-values, confidence intervals, or checks for nonlinearity/heterogeneity across datasets.

identified_claims.claim_text: A refined set of thirteen prerequisite skills for reading comprehension (RC), reorganized from prior work and cognitive theories, can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: Authors explicitly list 13 skills and describe refinements from Sugawara et al. (2017).
Textual grounding: mapping to textual entailment phenomena and cognitive dichotomies (retrieved vs generated; bridging vs elaboration).
uncertainty_flags: Operational boundaries between some skills (e.g., bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge vs elaboration) are fuzzy in the text and not exhaustively specified.
No formal validation (coverage, mutual exclusivity, or factor analysis) of the 13-item taxonomy is provided.

identified_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical/syntactic/traditional indices) and the number/types of prerequisite skills capture different aspects of dataset difficulty (reading ease vs comprehension/reasoning requirements).
evidence: The paper motivates the two axes from McNamara & Magliano (2009) and lists readability features derived from Vajjala & Meurers (2012).
Separate operationalizations: multi-label skills vs sentence-level readability features.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical separability depends on measurement choices; later analysis claims weak correlation but measurement dependencies (readability on selected sentences) complicate clean separability evidence.

identified_claims.claim_text: There is only a weak correlation between readability of contexts and the number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions: texts that are easy to read can yield difficult questions and vice versa.

Figures 3 and 4 depict dataset-level and per-question scatterplots with apparent cluster separation.
uncertainty_flags: Reported correlation range includes very small values; no p-values, confidence intervals, or tests for nonlinear relationships are provided.
Readability computed on annotator-selected sentences, creating dependence between skill labels and readability measures.
Possible heterogeneity across datasets; pooled correlations may obscure per-dataset patterns.

evidence: Figures 3 and 4 show dataset means and per-question plots that separate clusters.
Textual summaries in Results section describe dataset-specific profiles (QA4MRE high both, MCTest easy-read/hard-answer, SQuAD hard-read/easy-answer).
uncertainty_flags: Characterizations rely on 100-sample annotations per dataset; representativeness and sampling variability may shift region assignments.
No formal clustering or boundary definitions; observations remain descriptive.

Annotation protocol: three annotators, sentence selection, multi-label skill decisions.
uncertainty_flags: Agreement metric unspecified (percent agreement vs chance-corrected kappa); percent agreement can be misleading for skewed or multi-label data.
Agreement computed on 62-item subset, not full corpus; per-skill agreement and confusion matrices not provided.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotation procedure: annotators saw context, question, and answer jointly, selected sentences needed to answer, and labeled required prerequisite skills; readability metrics were computed only on the selected sentences.
evidence: Explicit description in Section 4.1: annotators select needed sentences and then label skills.
Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'
uncertainty_flags: This operational choice excludes evaluating sentence-selection competence and may bias readability to the annotators' selections; inter-annotator variability in selection not reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Dataset-level observations: QA4MRE highest in required skills and readability; MS MARCO relatively easy (many questions with <3 skills) but contains 'nonsense' questions; Who-did-What often requires ellipsis/bridging/elaboration due to its sourcing; NewsQA provides meta-information allowing filtering of nonsense.
evidence: Table 2: per-skill frequency percentages showing QA4MRE, Who-did-What, etc.
Table 3: distributions of number-of-skills and averages; Table 6: sentence counts/distances; textual interpretation in Results.

Sampling/selection could over- or under-estimate skill prevalence for each dataset.

identified_claims.claim_text: The two metric classes (readability and prerequisite skills) can guide curriculum-style dataset creation and system development steps: start with easy-to-read/easy-to-answer, progress to easy-to-read/hard-to-answer, then hard-to-read/hard-to-answer.

strengths.title: Clear theoretical motivation linking cognitive models to metrics
strengths.description: The paper grounds the dual-axis evaluation (skills vs readability) in established cognitive literature (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch) and entailment analyses, improving conceptual clarity.
evidence: Introduction and Section 2 explicitly cite McNamara and Magliano (2009), Kintsch (1993), and entailment literature to motivate metric classes.

strengths.title: Operationalized taxonomy and annotation protocol
strengths.description: The authors present a concrete 13-skill taxonomy and an annotation procedure (sentence selection + multi-label skill tagging) enabling reproducible data collection.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists 13 skills with descriptions; Section 4.1 describes the annotation steps and handling of multiple-choice and nonsense cases.

strengths.title: Multi-dataset empirical application and released resource
strengths.description: Annotation across six widely used RC datasets (100 items each) plus public release of labels provides a practical resource for the community and comparative insight.
evidence: Section 4.2 dataset choices and Section 5 results; authors state they will make annotations publicly available.

strengths.title: Transparent identification of dataset-specific phenomena
strengths.description: Results include per-dataset skill frequencies, number-of-skill distributions, and sentence-distance metrics that elucidate dataset construction effects (e.g., automated curation producing 'nonsense').
evidence: Tables 2–3 and Table 6; textual discussion in Results section about Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA filtering.

concerns.title: Readability measurement circularity via annotator sentence selection
concerns.description: Readability metrics were computed only on sentences annotators selected as 'needed' to answer questions; because skill labels and sentence selection were made jointly by annotators, readability becomes partially a function of annotator judgment rather than an independent corpus property. This can bias the measured correlation between readability and skill-count.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'
Section 4.1: annotators select sentences and label prerequisite skills.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute readability metrics both on (a) annotator-selected sentences (current) and (b) whole context texts for the same questions; report correlations for both operationalizations and analyze differences. Additionally, report inter-annotator agreement on sentence selection.

concerns.title: Insufficient reporting of annotation reliability
concerns.description: Inter-annotator agreement is summarized as a single percent (90.1%) on a 62-item subset without specification of the statistic (percent agreement vs. chance-corrected), no per-skill agreement, and no confusion matrices for multi-label decisions. This prevents assessment of annotation quality and label-specific reliability.
evidence: Section 5: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.' No kappa or per-skill numbers provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report chance-corrected agreement measures (Fleiss’ kappa or Krippendorff’s alpha) for multi-label annotations, per-skill agreement rates, confusion matrices, and sentence-selection agreement. If available, provide examples of disagreements to illustrate edge cases.

concerns.title: Limited statistical inference and robustness checks
concerns.description: Correlation analysis is based on Pearson coefficients with ranges reported but no p-values, confidence intervals, or tests for nonlinearity and heterogeneity. Pooling across heterogeneous datasets may mask differing relationships.
evidence: Section 5 reports Pearson correlations (0.025–0.416) in Table 5 but no inferential statistics beyond coefficient ranges; visual plots show clusters but no stratified tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide p-values and confidence intervals for reported correlations, compute Spearman rank correlations, and present dataset-stratified analyses. Consider regression models controlling for context length or genre and test for interaction effects.

concerns.title: Taxonomy validation and potential overlap
concerns.description: The 13-skill taxonomy is plausible but boundary conditions between skills (e.g., bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge) are not exhaustively specified or empirically validated (no factor analysis or practitioner validation), risking label ambiguity.
evidence: Section 3.1 definitions and the shared analysis note that certain skills may overlap and edge cases were not thoroughly specified.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a supplementary guide with numerous annotated examples per skill, run an expert validation or cognitive-informant study, and report any post-hoc analyses (e.g., co-occurrence matrices, PCA/FA) that probe whether skills form distinct factors.

concerns.title: Sampling representativeness for dataset-level claims
concerns.description: Using 100 random questions per dataset may be insufficient for heterogeneous datasets; sampling procedures differ per dataset (Appendix A) and may bias dataset-level profiles.
evidence: Section 4.2 states 100 questions sampled per dataset and Appendix A details sampling variations (e.g., paragraphs, tasks, filters).
Shared analysis flags representativeness concerns.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify sampling seeds/methods, report bootstrapped confidence intervals over repeated random samples, and, if possible, increase sample size or stratify sampling by document/topic/length to test robustness.

concerns.title: Ambiguous treatment and quantification of 'nonsense'/'no-answer' cases
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges nonsense/no-answer items and that datasets differ in prevalence, but the operationalization, annotator instructions, and impact of excluding or including these items are not systematically analyzed.
evidence: Section 4.1 mentions annotators could mark nonsense; Section 5 reports per-dataset nonsense percentages but does not present sensitivity analyses.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide annotation guidelines for nonsense/no-answer, per-dataset prevalence tables, and sensitivity analyses showing results with and without these items.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors adopt Vajjala & Meurers' top features for human readability, applying them to annotator-selected sentences for RC-focused analysis.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2 and Figure 2 cite this work as feature source.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior dataset analysis highlighting dataset quality issues (CNN/Daily Mail unsolvable questions) and precedent for sampling decisions.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Chen et al. analyze dataset solvability and noise; current paper adds skill taxonomy and readability axes for richer characterization.
comparable_works.source_trace: Introduction, Section 2, and Section 4.2 reference Chen et al. regarding dataset quality and sampling considerations.

comparable_works.relevance: Cognitive grounding motivating the two-axis decomposition (strategic comprehension vs text ease of processing).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides theoretical justification rather than empirical overlap; current work operationalizes their dichotomy for RC dataset analysis.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in Introduction and Section 2 as theoretical basis.

uncertainty_flags: Annotation reliability: reliance on a single percent agreement figure without chance-corrected metrics or per-skill breakdown.
Measurement dependence: readability computed on annotator-selected sentences induces potential circularity and selection bias.
Sampling concerns: 100 items per dataset may not represent heterogeneous corpora; sampling methods differ per dataset.
Statistical reporting: Pearson correlations provided without p-values, CIs, or nonparametric alternatives; pooled analyses may mask dataset heterogeneity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper operationalizes RC difficulty along two axes: prerequisite skills (a 13-item taxonomy adapted from prior work and cognitive theory) and readability (ten NLP features from Vajjala & Meurers 2012). Three annotators labeled 100 randomly sampled questions from six RC datasets: they selected sentences deemed necessary to answer each question, marked required skills (multi-label), and flagged 'nonsense' or 'no-answer' items. Readability metrics were computed only on annotator-selected sentences. Analyses report per-dataset skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, readability summaries, and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability (weak correlations reported, 0.025–0.416). Inter-annotator agreement is reported as 90.1% on a 62-question subset. The paper argues that the two metric classes capture different aspects of difficulty, are only weakly correlated, and that datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space; it releases the annotation resource to guide dataset construction and curriculum-style development. Primary methodological dependencies are: (1) validity and coverage of the 13-skill taxonomy; (2) annotation reliability for multi-label skill assignment and sentence selection; (3) representativeness of the 100-question samples per dataset; (4) appropriateness of applying human-focused readability metrics to annotator-selected sentences; and (5) use of Pearson correlation without reported p-values or checks for non-linearity or confounds. Several pieces of evidence are missing or underspecified (per-skill agreement, chance-corrected reliability, exact correlation tables with p-values, sampling seeds, annotation guidelines/examples, sensitivity analyses recomputing readability on whole contexts, and robustness to alternative difficulty proxies).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper frames RC difficulty as two partially independent dimensions: (1) prerequisite skills required to produce the entailment from context to (question,answer) and (2) text readability (lexical/syntactic measures). Building on prior cognitive and entailment literature, the authors (a) refine an existing skills taxonomy into 13 prerequisite skills mapped to entailment/psychology distinctions (bridging vs elaboration, retrieval vs generated inference), (b) operationalize readability via ten NLP features (Vajjala & Meurers' top features) computed on annotator-selected sentences, (c) collect multi-label skill annotations and sentence-selection for 100 sampled questions across six RC datasets, and (d) compute skill-counts, per-skill frequencies, readability scores, and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability. From the observed weak correlations (Pearson 0.025–0.416) and dataset-level distributions the authors conclude that readability and required skills capture different aspects of difficulty and that datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space, motivating dataset-specific diagnosis and a curriculum-style progression for system development. The reasoning depends critically on (i) the 13-skill taxonomy being sufficiently discriminative and well operationalized for annotators, (ii) the reliability of multi-label annotations and sentence-selection, (iii) the representativeness of the 100-question samples per dataset, and (iv) the choice to compute readability on annotator-selected sentences rather than whole contexts. The empirical findings are internally coherent and plausible but are sensitive to those methodological choices; some claims (e.g., high inter-annotator agreement, dataset-region assignments, and general implications for curriculum learning) require additional reporting and robustness checks to be convincing beyond the sampled subsets.

Readability comparisons (Table 4) and Figures 3–4 visualize joint properties.

strengths.title: Resource release intention and practical guidance
strengths.description: Authors state intent to release annotations and suggest pragmatic uses (dataset construction, curriculum), increasing utility for the community.
evidence: "We annotate six existing RC datasets... and make the results publicly available." (Contributions).
Discussion section outlines curriculum-style usage.

concerns.title: Taxonomy validation and label separability under-specified
concerns.description: The 13-skill taxonomy is described and motivated by prior theory, but the manuscript lacks formal validation that skills are mutually exclusive, exhaustive for RC phenomena, and consistently interpretable by annotators; definitions for edge cases are sparse.
evidence: Sec. 3.1 provides definitions but the shared analysis notes potential overlap (bridging vs elaboration, meta-knowledge vs elaboration).
Uncertainty flag: limited formal validation of taxonomy completeness or mutual exclusivity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide (a) annotation guidelines with decision rules and examples for each skill and typical boundary cases; (b) a small validation study showing per-skill inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Fleiss' or Cohen's kappa per label); (c) confusion matrices to reveal overlapping labels.

concerns.title: Annotation reliability reporting is insufficient
concerns.description: Inter-annotator agreement is reported as a single percent (90.1%) on a 62-question subset without chance-corrected measures or per-label agreements, leaving doubts about reliability for multi-label annotations and sentence selection.
evidence: "The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions." (Sec. 5)
Shared analysis notes lack of Cohen/Fleiss kappa and per-skill agreement statistics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report chance-corrected agreement statistics (Fleiss' kappa for multi-rater multi-label or label-wise Cohen's kappa), provide per-skill agreement, and report agreement on sentence-selection decisions (e.g., IOU-style overlap). If some skills show low agreement, revise guidelines or collapse/merge ambiguous categories.

concerns.title: Readability measurement depends on annotator-selected sentences
concerns.description: Computing readability only on sentences annotators selected conflates selection choices with textual complexity measures and may bias correlations between readability and skill-count.
evidence: "We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions." (Sec. 3.2)
Shared analysis: selection variability not reported; selection may under- or over-estimate true reading difficulty.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include sensitivity analyses computing readability on (a) whole contexts, (b) annotator-union of selected sentences, and (c) randomly chosen sentences of similar length; compare correlations and report differences to show the robustness of the weak-correlation finding.

concerns.title: Sampling size and representativeness not rigorously justified
concerns.description: Selecting 100 questions per dataset follows precedent but may be insufficient for heterogeneous datasets; sampling strategy per dataset and potential topic/length skews are not fully characterized.
evidence: "We randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset... This amount ... as performed by Chen et al. (2016)." (Sec. 4.2)
Appendix A describes sampling but not diagnostics of representativeness.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide exploratory diagnostics: compare sampled vs full-dataset distributions for key covariates (context length, topic, answer type); if feasible, increase sample size for datasets with high heterogeneity or stratify sampling (by article length, question type). Report sensitivity of main results to sampling.

concerns.title: Statistical reporting of correlations is incomplete
concerns.description: Correlation results are reported as coefficient ranges but without p-values, confidence intervals, or tests for nonlinearity and dataset heterogeneity; Pearson correlation may not capture the relationship structure.
evidence: "Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416..." (Sec. 5(iv))
Shared analysis noted missing p-values and possibility of non-linear relationships.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report full correlation tables with Pearson/Spearman coefficients, p-values, and 95% CIs. Perform dataset-stratified analyses, test for nonlinearity (e.g., GAMs or rank correlations), and consider multivariate controls (context length, genre).

concerns.title: Curriculum prescription remains speculative
concerns.description: Recommendation to arrange datasets along the two-axis continuum for curriculum learning is appealing, but the paper offers no empirical validation that such curricula improve system learning.
evidence: Discussion suggests stepwise progression using measured dataset properties (Sec. 6).
No experiments demonstrating curriculum gains included.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Frame the curriculum suggestion as a hypothesis and, if possible, add a small preliminary experiment (e.g., train a model on easy-to-read/easy-to-answer then fine-tune on harder regimes) or cite plans and constraints for future empirical validation.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper refines and expands Sugawara et al.'s taxonomy (from 10 to 13 skills) and broadens dataset coverage from two datasets to six; it claims stronger theoretical grounding in entailment and cognitive models.

comparable_works.relevance: Cognitive theory motivating the two-axis framing (strategic comprehension vs ease of processing).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used as conceptual foundation rather than empirical benchmark; the paper translates theory into operational metrics for dataset analysis.

uncertainty_flags: Taxonomy boundaries ambiguous for some skills (bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge overlap).
Inter-annotator agreement reported only as percent on a small subset; no chance-corrected or per-skill reliability reported.
Readability stats computed on annotator-selected sentences — selection variability not quantified and may confound results.
Correlation analysis reports coefficient ranges but lacks p-values, CIs, and tests for nonlinearity or dataset-specific heterogeneity.
Sampling 100 questions per dataset may be insufficient for datasets with large internal diversity; sampling diagnostics are limited.
Treatment and prevalence of 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' labels require fuller exposition (operational definitions and impact on analyses).
alternative_interpretations: The weak correlation between readability and skill-count could be an artifact of computing readability on annotator-selected sentences (which tend to be locally informative and possibly less complex) rather than whole documents; whole-context readability might show different relationships.

Skill-count may not equate to cognitive or algorithmic difficulty uniformly across skills: some skills (e.g., bridging) might be harder than others, so simple counts obscure weight/heterogeneity of skill difficulty.

High percent agreement may mask label imbalance or lottery agreement; per-label reliability could reveal that only a subset of skills is reliably annotated, meaning reported frequency patterns are driven by a few well-agreed labels.
Dataset-specific sampling choices (e.g., filtering NewsQA via meta-info, MS MARCO contextual selection) could bias which items were included and thus the observed dataset-region assignments.
transparency_notes: Request release of: (a) full annotation dataset (question IDs, selected sentence indices, multi-label skill vectors per annotator), (b) annotation guidelines/instruction text and examples, (c) random seed and sampling code used for selecting 100 questions per dataset, and (d) analysis scripts for readability computation and correlation tables (including Table 5 raw values).
Ask authors to report per-skill and sentence-selection inter-annotator agreement, confusion matrices, and labeling time or annotator notes capturing disagreement types.
Recommend publishing Table 5 full statistics (coefficients, p-values, sample sizes) and alternative correlation metrics (Spearman) and including robustness checks (whole-context readability).

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper sits in an incremental space: it refines an existing skills taxonomy and combines it with established readability metrics applied across multiple datasets. Novelty is real in the integrated operationalization and cross-dataset application, but novelty does not guarantee validity—the empirical conclusions depend on methodological choices (annotation reliability, sentence-selection, sampling) that require further validation.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If per-skill inter-annotator agreement is high (chance-corrected), demonstrating taxonomy reliability across annotators and datasets.
If sensitivity analyses show that readability–skill correlations hold (or remain weak) when computing readability on whole contexts and when stratifying by dataset/genre.

If skill-count correlates with independent difficulty measures (system performance degradation, human response times, or held-out human difficulty ratings), supporting the assumption that skill-count maps to difficulty.
If expanded sampling (or stratified sampling) preserves dataset-region assignments, showing robustness against sample bias.

evidence: Paper expands Sugawara's 10 skills to 13 with entailment/cognitive grounding (Sec. 3.1).
Applies metrics to six datasets with annotation protocol and comparative analysis (Sec. 4–5).
uncertainty_flags: Strength of contribution depends on taxonomy validation and annotation reliability.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The dataset labels and cross-dataset diagnostics could be practically valuable for dataset curation and curriculum design, but utility depends on release quality and additional validation linking metrics to system/human difficulty.
evidence: Authors state plans to publish annotations and highlight curriculum learning applications (Sec. 6).
Empirical tables and visualizations illustrate dataset differences (Tables 2–3, Figures 3–4).
uncertainty_flags: Actual downstream utility untested in the manuscript; prescriptive claims are not empirically demonstrated.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The methodological choices (annotator-selected sentences, 100-sample per dataset, use of Pearson correlation) are defensible but require additional robustness checks and fuller statistical reporting to be convincing.
evidence: Annotation procedure described, but reliability metrics incomplete; correlation results reported without p-values.
Shared analysis and chaining notes recommend sensitivity analyses.
uncertainty_flags: Missing robustness analyses and complete statistical reporting.

confidence_interval.rationale: Moderate-to-high confidence that the paper offers a useful incremental contribution (refined taxonomy + cross-dataset annotation + descriptive analysis). However, confidence is reduced by methodological gaps (annotation reliability reporting, sampling representativeness, and limited statistical reporting). Filling those gaps as suggested would push confidence toward the upper bound.

prior_stage_inputs: Shared analysis: extracted claims C1–C8, identified assumptions A1–A9, argument_focus, contribution_targets, uncertainty_flags, and chaining_notes.
Manuscript context (148.pdf) with sections: Intro, Related Work, Metrics (3.1/3.2), Annotation (4), Results (5), Discussion (6), Appendices A/B.
Tables & figures referenced in shared analysis: Table 2/3 (skill frequencies, #skills), Table 4 (readability metrics summary), Table 5 (correlations), Figures 3/4 (FK grade vs skills).
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper advances an operational two-axis framework to characterize reading-comprehension (RC) datasets: (1) a refined taxonomy of 13 'prerequisite skills' intended to approximate the cognitive/entailment functions required to answer RC questions; and (2) a set of readability metrics (top features from Vajjala & Meurers 2012) applied to annotator-selected sentences. The central reasoning chain is: (P1) reading comprehension difficulty decomposes into text-ease (readability) and strategic comprehension (skills), per McNamara & Magliano (2009); (P2) prior skill taxonomies are incomplete or underspecified, so reorganize into 13 skills grounded in textual-entailment and cognitive theory; (P3) annotate representative samples (100 items × 6 datasets) to measure per-question skill labels and sentence-level readability; (P4) compute dataset-level summaries and correlations to test whether readability and skill-count align; (C) report that readability and required skills are weakly correlated, datasets occupy distinct joint regions, and that the annotation resource and taxonomy can guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development. The empirical chain relies on (i) the 13-skill operationalization (multi-label annotation), (ii) annotator sentence-selection which constrains where readability is measured, and (iii) Pearson correlations and descriptive plots to support the weak-association claim. The paper's contribution is primarily empirical (annotation + dataset analysis) with a conceptual reframing of difficulty along orthogonal axes and a practical recommendation for curriculum ordering of datasets.
logical_argument_graph: McNamara&Magliano(2009) + textual-entailment literature -> conceptual separation: readability vs prerequisite skills
Sugawara et al. (2017) provisional taxonomy -> reorganize and extend -> 13 prerequisite skills (C1)
Annotators see (context, question, answer) -> select 'necessary' sentences -> label multi-label skills -> compute readability on selection (C6)
Aggregate annotations across 6 datasets (100 samples each) -> compute skill frequencies, #skills distributions, readability summaries (Tables 2–4)
Compute Pearson correlations between #skills and readability metrics -> observe weak coefficients (0.025–0.416) (C3)
Visualize joint space (FK grade vs avg #skills) -> datasets occupy distinct regions (C4)
High reported overall agreement (90.1% on 62-sample subset) -> claim annotation reliability (C5)
Therefore: readability and skill-count capture different aspects; resource can guide curriculum-style dataset/system development (C2, C8)

identified_claims.claim_text: A refined set of thirteen prerequisite skills for reading comprehension (RC), reorganized from prior work and cognitive theories, can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: "By refining Sugawara et al. (2017)’s ten reading comprehension skills, we reorganized thirteen prerequisite skills in total..." (Sec. 3.1)
Complete list of 13 skills and explicit ties to textual entailment and psychology (Kintsch; McNamara & Magliano) in Sec. 3.1.
uncertainty_flags: Operational definitions for some skills (bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge boundaries) may overlap and are not exhaustively disambiguated.
No formal validation (e.g., expert adjudication, pilot coverage study) of taxonomy completeness or mutual exclusivity reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical/syntactic/traditional indices) and the number/types of prerequisite skills capture different aspects of dataset difficulty (reading ease vs comprehension/reasoning requirements).
evidence: "Based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)’s depiction of text comprehension, we adopted two classes for the evaluation of RC datasets: prerequisite skills and readability." (Sec. 3)
Separate operationalizations: 13-skill multi-label annotation vs top-ten readability metrics (Figure 2).
uncertainty_flags: Separability is partially an operational choice; empirical separability depends on metric choices and annotation procedures, which could induce artificial decoupling.

identified_claims.claim_text: There is only a weak correlation between readability of contexts and the number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions: texts that are easy to read can yield difficult questions and vice versa.
evidence: "Table 5 presents Pearson’s correlation coefficients... Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values." (Sec. 5(iv))
Figures 3 and 4 showing FK grade vs average/individual #skills and descriptive discussion (Sec. 5).
uncertainty_flags: Pearson coefficients reported but p-values, confidence intervals, and effect-size interpretations are not shown in the paper extract.
Readability is measured on annotator-selected sentences; selection variability could attenuate or bias correlations.

identified_claims.claim_text: Different existing RC datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space of readability and prerequisite-skill difficulty (examples: QA4MRE: hard-to-read & hard-to-answer; MCTest: easy-to-read but often hard-to-answer; SQuAD: hard-to-read but relatively easy-to-answer).
evidence: "QA4MRE was relatively difficult both to read and to answer, and SQuAD was difficult to read but easy to answer." (Sec. 5(iv))
Figures 3/4 visualizations and dataset-level score summaries in Tables 2–3 and text description.
uncertainty_flags: Regions are descriptive; boundaries are not formally defined and rely on the 100-sample-per-dataset selection.
Dataset-level placements are sensitive to sampling, sentence-selection, and metric configurations.

identified_claims.claim_text: Manual annotation of 100 examples per dataset (six datasets) produced high inter-annotator agreement (reported 90.1% on a random subset), and the resulting labels are released to guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.
evidence: "We asked three annotators..." (Sec. 4.1)
"The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions." (Sec. 5)
uncertainty_flags: Percent agreement metric unspecified (percent agreement vs kappa). No per-skill agreement, confusion matrices, or chance-corrected reliability reported.
Agreement computed on 62-item subset; representativeness across datasets or labels unclear.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotation procedure: annotators saw context, question, and answer jointly, selected sentences needed to answer, and labeled required prerequisite skills; readability metrics were computed only on the selected sentences.
evidence: "The annotators then selected sentences that needed to be read to answer the question and decided if each prerequisite skill was required." (Sec. 4.1)
"We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions." (Sec. 3.2)
uncertainty_flags: This operational choice decouples readability from whole-context complexity and intentionally excludes sentence-selection competence; inter-annotator variability in selection not reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Dataset-level observations: QA4MRE highest in required skills and readability; MS MARCO relatively easy (many questions with <3 skills) but contains 'nonsense' questions; Who-did-What often requires ellipsis/bridging/elaboration due to its sourcing; NewsQA provides meta-information allowing filtering of nonsense.
evidence: Table 2 and Table 3 frequency summaries (skill frequencies and number-of-skills distributions).
Textual summary: per-dataset narratives in Sec. 5, e.g., "MS MARCO and Who-did-What received relatively high scores [for nonsense]..."
uncertainty_flags: Sampling of 100 items may not capture heterogeneity; 'nonsense' label definitions depend on annotator judgment and prevalence across full datasets not reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: The two metric classes (readability and prerequisite skills) can guide curriculum-style dataset creation and system development steps: start with easy-to-read/easy-to-answer, progress to easy-to-read/hard-to-answer, then hard-to-read/hard-to-answer.
evidence: "One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset... appropriate datasets can be prepared for every step by measuring their properties using the metrics of this study." (Sec. 6)
uncertainty_flags: This is a prescription; no empirical curriculum experiments are provided to validate that ordering improves learning or transfer.
Effectiveness depends on metric reliability and dataset representativeness.

strengths.title: Clear conceptual two-axis framing
strengths.description: The paper articulates a defendable conceptual separation between text readability and prerequisite reasoning skills, grounded in cognitive literature and textual-entailment theory.
evidence: Sec. 1 links McNamara & Magliano (2009) and Kintsch (1993) to motivate two metric classes.
Sec. 3 explicitly operationalizes both classes and maps them to concrete metrics (13 skills and top readability features).

strengths.title: Practical, reproducible annotation protocol
strengths.description: Annotation procedure is explicit: joint presentation of (context, question, answer), sentence selection, and multi-label skill assignment; this allows replication and reuse.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes the annotation flow and multi-label format.
Appendix A details dataset sampling procedures.

strengths.title: Cross-dataset empirical analysis and released labels
strengths.description: Annotation across six diverse RC datasets (100 items each) and dataset-level summaries provide comparative insights not available in single-dataset analyses.
evidence: Tables 2–3 present comparative skill and #skill distributions across QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, WDW, MARCO, NewsQA.
Authors state that the annotated results will be publicly released.

strengths.title: Actionable downstream suggestion (curriculum)
strengths.description: Paper connects dataset measurement to curriculum-style development for RC systems, giving an actionable direction for dataset selection and system training phases.
evidence: Discussion in Section 6 advocates a step-wise dataset ordering aligned to the two axes.

concerns.title: Taxonomy validity and boundary clarity
concerns.description: The 13-skill taxonomy is plausible but lacks formal validation: boundaries between several skills (bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge vs elaboration; object tracking vs clause relations) are not exhaustively defined or empirically tested for mutual exclusivity.
evidence: Shared analysis: uncertainty flags note that operational definitions for some skills may overlap.
Sec. 3.1 lists skills with some justification, but no validation study or expert adjudication is described.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide (a) a short rubric with edge-case examples for each of the 13 skills, (b) pilot adjudication by domain experts or linguists showing coverage/overlap statistics, and (c) per-skill confusion matrices computed from annotation disagreements.

concerns.title: Annotation reliability reporting insufficient
concerns.description: Inter-annotator agreement is reported as a single 90.1% percent-agreement on a 62-item subset; chance-corrected agreement (Fleiss' kappa/Cohen's kappa) and per-skill agreement statistics are missing, which obscures reliability for multi-label annotation.
evidence: "The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions." (Sec. 5) — no kappa or per-label agreement.
Shared analysis notes: percent agreement can be inflated for skewed labels.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report kappa/Fleiss' kappa for multi-rater agreement, per-skill agreement, and confusion matrices; increase the reliability sample or report bootstrapped confidence intervals to show stability.

concerns.title: Sampling representativeness and sample size justification
concerns.description: The study uses 100 randomly selected questions per dataset (development/gold splits). For heterogeneous datasets, 100 samples may not capture distributional variation; Appendix A sampling heuristics vary by dataset and may introduce selection bias.
evidence: Appendix A details different sampling strategies (e.g., one question per paragraph for SQuAD), and shared analysis flags sample-size sufficiency concerns.
Results (dataset-region placement) are sensitive to sample representativeness.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide sampling diagnostics: distributions of topic, length, and answer types in sampled vs full datasets; where feasible, expand sample size or stratify sampling (by article length, answer type) and show sensitivity analyses.

concerns.title: Readability measurement conditional on annotator-selected sentences
concerns.description: Readability features are computed only on annotator-selected sentences deemed 'needed' to answer the question; inter-annotator variability in selection and the choice to exclude whole-context measures can bias readability estimates and thus the correlation analysis.
evidence: "We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions." (Sec. 3.2)
Shared analysis: selection variability not reported and may confound readability–skill relationships.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator overlap statistics for selected sentences; compute readability both on selected sentences and on whole contexts as a robustness check; show whether correlations change when using alternative selection aggregations (union/intersection).

concerns.title: Correlation analysis reporting and statistical robustness
concerns.description: Pearson correlation coefficients are summarized (range 0.025–0.416) but p-values, confidence intervals, dataset-stratified significance, and checks for non-linear associations (Spearman, subgroup patterns) are not provided; Pearson may understate non-linear or heteroskedastic relationships.
evidence: "Table 5 presents Pearson’s correlation coefficients..." but shared analysis notes missing p-values and dataset-specific details.
Figures 3/4 are descriptive; no statistical tests for clustering or heterogeneity are presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full Table 5 with p-values and CI; add Spearman correlations and scatterplots with LOESS fits; run dataset-stratified analyses and tests for heterogeneity and report effect sizes.

concerns.title: Treatment and operationalization of 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' cases
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' items (especially in MARCO and WDW), but the annotation criteria, prevalence across full datasets, and how such items are handled in analyses (included/excluded) are not sufficiently quantified.
evidence: Sec. 4.1: annotators could mark 'nonsense'; Sec. 5 notes variable nonsense frequencies per dataset.
Shared analysis calls out that definitions and thresholds are unclear.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide the annotation instruction text for 'nonsense'/'no-answer' decisions, prevalence tables per full dataset, and sensitivity analyses with/without these items included in correlation and summary statistics.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides theoretical basis; current paper operationalizes this split for RC dataset analysis.

comparable_works.relevance: Critical analysis of dataset quality (CNN/Daily Mail) and sample-size precedent (100 samples referenced).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used to justify sample-size sufficiency and to motivate caution about automated dataset curation.

Inter-annotator reliability reported as a single percent-agreement on 62 items without chance correction or per-skill metrics.
Readability measured only on annotator-selected sentences; sentence-selection variability not reported.
Pearson correlation coefficients presented without p-values, CIs, or tests for non-linearity and heterogeneity.

alternative_interpretations: Weak correlations between readability and skill-count may arise from measurement choices (sentence-level readability, specific readability features) rather than a true independence of text complexity and reasoning difficulty.

Dataset-level clustering in figures could reflect sampling artifacts (e.g., topical or length biases in the 100-sample selection) or design quirks (e.g., WDW cloze-style sourcing) rather than intrinsic dataset properties.
