transparency_notes: Please release full annotation guidelines, the annotation interface screenshots, and the exact instruction text used to train annotators (critical for reproducing sentence-selection and 'nonsense' judgments).
Publish per-item labels, per-skill label distributions, per-skill confusion matrices, and the full Table 5 with p-values and confidence intervals.
Share sampling code, random seeds, and selection scripts (Appendix A references sampling but code would enable verification).
Clarify the exact agreement metric used for the reported 90.1% and provide per-dataset and per-skill agreement stats.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The conceptual framing—operationalizing RC difficulty as orthogonal dimensions of prerequisite skills and readability, then applying sentence-level readability to annotator-selected sentences—is novel in scope and application. However, novelty alone does not establish validity: the paper needs robustness checks, formal taxonomy validation, and stronger reliability reporting before results can be treated as definitive.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If per-skill inter-annotator agreement (kappa) is shown to be high and confusion matrices show clear separability, the taxonomy will be credible and generalizable.
If readability-vs-skill correlations remain weak under robustness checks (whole-context readability, Spearman correlations, stratified samples), the core empirical claim is strengthened.
If curriculum-style training experiments demonstrate measurable transfer gains when datasets are ordered by the proposed axes, the practical utility claim is validated.
If larger, stratified samples across more dataset types (including cloze/anonymized variants) reproduce dataset-region patterns, the joint-space framing will generalize.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The two-axis decomposition linked to an operational multi-label skills taxonomy and sentence-level readability is a fresh framing that can expose dataset-level tradeoffs not captured by simple metadata or question/answer type labels.
evidence: Integration of cognitive theory (McNamara & Magliano) and entailment typology to reorganize skill taxonomy (Sec. 3.1).
Empirical application across six diverse RC datasets with a released annotated subset.
uncertainty_flags: Relies on unvalidated taxonomy and limited reliability reporting; empirical claims need robustness checks.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Extension of existing work rather than radical departure
novelty_lenses.rationale: Builds directly on Sugawara et al. and known readability feature sets; the novelty is in scale and framing rather than in entirely new theory or measurement techniques.
evidence: Taxonomy is a reorganization/extension of Sugawara et al. (2017).
Readability features are drawn from Vajjala & Meurers (2012).
uncertainty_flags: Even if incremental in components, combining them and applying sentence-level readability to annotator-selected evidence is still uncommon and potentially valuable.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in the descriptive observations and the paper's conceptual framing (lower risk) but less confident that the empirical claims are fully validated as presented due to methodological concerns (taxonomy validation, inter-annotator reliability measures, sampling robustness, and incomplete statistical reporting). Improvements in those areas would raise confidence toward the upper bound.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper operationalizes RC difficulty along two axes—(A) prerequisite skills (a refined 13-item taxonomy derived from prior work and cognitive theory) and (B) readability (top linguistic features from Vajjala & Meurers, 2012). The authors annotate 100 sampled questions from six RC datasets: annotators select minimal sentences necessary to answer each question, multi-label the applicable prerequisite skills, and mark 'nonsense'/'no-answer' items. Readability metrics are computed only on annotator-selected sentences. The main empirical claim is that readability and the number/types of prerequisite skills are weakly correlated (Pearson r range reported 0.025–0.416), and datasets occupy different regions in the joint space (examples: QA4MRE high readability+skills, MCTest easy-read but hard-questions, SQuAD hard-read but easier-to-answer). The paper reports overall inter-annotator agreement 90.1% on a 62-question subset and releases the annotations. Strengths include clear conceptual framing, operationalized annotation protocol, cross-dataset empirical application, and a released resource. Core concerns: taxonomy boundary clarity and validation; annotation reliability metrics insufficient (single percent agreement, no chance-corrected or per-skill statistics); potential circularity/measurement dependence because readability was computed on annotator-selected sentences (sentence-selection variability unreported); sampling representativeness (100 items/dataset, heterogeneous sampling across datasets); limited statistical reporting (no p-values, CIs, or non-parametric checks; Pearson may miss nonlinear or subgroup effects); and underreported handling/impact of 'nonsense'/'no-answer' labels. I differentiate claims that are well-supported by the manuscript's evidence from those that are partially supported or overstated, and I flag uncertainties and actionable checks to strengthen the paper.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Human text comprehension theory (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch) motivates two axes: strategic comprehension (skills) and text ease (readability).
P2: Prior skill taxonomies (Sugawara et al.) are incomplete; authors refine into 13 prerequisite skills grounded in entailment distinctions and psychology.
P3: Annotators select minimal sentences needed per question and multi-label required skills; readability is computed on selected sentences.
P4: Aggregate per-dataset skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, and readability feature summaries are computed; Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability are reported.
C1: Readability and prerequisite-skill dimensions capture different aspects of difficulty and are only weakly correlated (empirical evidence: Pearson r range 0.025–0.416).
C2: Datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space (qualitative placements: QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, etc.).
C3: The annotation resource and two-axis metrics can guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.

identified_claims.claim_text: A refined set of thirteen prerequisite skills for RC (derived from prior work and cognitive theories) can be used to annotate questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: Authors present a 13-item list and tie items to prior literature (Sugawara et al., Kintsch, Dagan et al.).
Annotation protocol used those 13 skills in labeling 600 questions.
uncertainty_flags: No formal validation of taxonomy completeness, discriminative power, or mutual exclusivity is provided.
Operational boundaries for overlapping skills (e.g., bridging vs. elaboration; meta-knowledge vs. elaboration) are described but not exhaustively exemplified or empirically adjudicated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics and the number/types of prerequisite skills capture different aspects of dataset difficulty (reading ease vs comprehension/reasoning requirements).
evidence: Theoretical grounding: McNamara & Magliano's two-aspect model.
Empirical observation: datasets like MCTest show low readability but require multiple skills.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical separation depends on choice of readability features and the skill taxonomy; sensitivity tests absent.
Readability was measured only on sentences selected by annotators, coupling the two metrics.

identified_claims.claim_text: There is only a weak correlation between readability of contexts and the number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions.
evidence: Reported Pearson correlations range 0.025–0.416 (Table 5 referenced).
Figures 3 and 4 visually show dataset-specific distributions with apparent separation.
uncertainty_flags: No p-values, CIs, or tests for nonlinearity are provided; reported r-range includes trivially small values.
Readability computed on annotator-selected sentences; sentence-selection variability could bias correlations.
Pooling across datasets may mask heterogeneity; dataset-stratified inference sparse.

identified_claims.claim_text: Different RC datasets occupy distinct regions in the joint space of readability and prerequisite-skill difficulty (examples: QA4MRE: hard-to-read & hard-to-answer; MCTest: easy-to-read but often hard-to-answer; SQuAD: hard-to-read but relatively easy-to-answer).
evidence: Figure 3 (dataset means) and Figure 4 (per-question scatter) show separable clusters for sampled questions.
Textual descriptions and per-dataset tables (Tables 2–3) support dataset-specific profiles.
uncertainty_flags: Descriptions are sample-based (100 items/dataset) and qualitative; no formal clustering or statistical separation test.
Representativeness of samples and dependence on chosen readability/skill metrics may change region assignments.

identified_claims.claim_text: Manual annotation of 100 examples per dataset (six datasets) produced high inter-annotator agreement (reported 90.1% on a random 62-question subset), and the resulting labels can guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development.
evidence: Reported inter-annotator agreement: 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.
Annotation procedure: three annotators, sentence selection and multi-label skill marking.
uncertainty_flags: Agreement metric unspecified (percent agreement reported) and computed only on 62/600 items; no chance-corrected measure (e.g., Fleiss/Kappa) or per-skill agreement/confusion matrices.
How disagreements were adjudicated or whether agreement varied by dataset/skill is unreported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotators saw context, question, and answer jointly; they selected sentences needed to answer and labeled required prerequisite skills. Readability metrics were computed only on the selected sentences.
evidence: "The annotators then selected sentences that needed to be read to answer the question and decided if each prerequisite skill was required."
"We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions."
uncertainty_flags: Sentence-selection variability and its inter-annotator agreement are not reported; this step couples skill labels and readability computation, opening a circularity risk.
By design the method cannot evaluate sentence-selection competence; consequences for assessing system retrieval ability are acknowledged but not empirically addressed.

identified_claims.claim_text: Dataset-level observations: QA4MRE highest in required skills and readability; MS MARCO relatively easy; Who-did-What requires ellipsis/bridging/elaboration; NewsQA provides meta-information enabling filtering of nonsense.
evidence: Table 2 skill frequencies and Table 3 skill-count distributions.
Text narrative summarizing per-dataset findings (e.g., QA4MRE high, MS MARCO many <3 skills).
uncertainty_flags: Sampling scheme differences (e.g., SQuAD sampling one question per paragraph) and small sample size per dataset may bias these frequencies.
'Nonsense' prevalence depends on annotator judgments and dataset preprocessing described in Appendix A; thresholds and inter-annotator variation unreported.

identified_claims.claim_text: The two metric classes can guide curriculum-style dataset construction and system development (start easy-read/easy-answer → easy-read/hard-answer → hard-read/hard-answer).
evidence: "One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset... Appropriate datasets can be prepared for every step by measuring their properties using the metrics of this study."
uncertainty_flags: This is a prescriptive claim without empirical validation in the paper (no controlled experiments showing curriculum yields improved learning).
Effectiveness depends on annotation reliability and whether the axes capture relevant difficulty for model learning, which remain partially validated.

strengths.title: Clear theoretical framing linking cognitive models to dataset metrics
strengths.description: The paper grounds its two-axis framework (prerequisite skills vs readability) in established cognitive and textual-entailment theory (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch; Dagan et al.), providing a coherent conceptual bridge from psychology to dataset analysis.
evidence: Sections 1–3 cite McNamara & Magliano (2009), Kintsch (1993), and Dagan et al. (2013) to justify the two classes.
3.1 maps skills to entailment phenomena and psychological distinctions (bridging vs elaboration).

strengths.title: Operationalized annotation protocol with sentence-selection and multi-label skills
strengths.description: The authors provide a reproducible annotation procedure where annotators jointly see context/question/answer, select necessary sentences, and multi-label prerequisite skills — enabling fine-grained per-question analysis.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes annotator steps and allowed labels (including 'nonsense').
Readability metrics are computed on annotator-selected sentences, matching the intended operationalization.

strengths.title: Cross-dataset empirical application and public release of annotations
strengths.description: Applying the metrics to six diverse RC datasets (100 samples each) and releasing annotations makes an immediately useful resource for dataset diagnosis and follow-up studies.
evidence: Sections 4.2 and 5 describe datasets and present Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–4.
Authors state they make annotated results publicly available.

concerns.title: Taxonomy boundary clarity and formal validation missing
concerns.description: The 13-skill taxonomy is plausible and well-motivated but lacks formal validation: no held-out adjudication, inter-skill confusion analysis, or evidence that the set is complete and mutually discriminative for RC phenomena.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists skills and motivates them, but shared analysis notes potential overlaps (bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge vs elaboration).
No empirical validation study or examples resolving boundary cases are provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide (a) annotation guidelines with boundary examples; (b) per-skill agreement and confusion matrix on the annotated subset; (c) a short validation on external questions or adjudicated cases demonstrating coverage/mutual exclusivity.

concerns.title: Annotation reliability underreported (percent agreement only)
concerns.description: Reporting a single percent-agreement (90.1% on 62 items) is insufficient for multi-label, multi-annotator tasks: chance-corrected measures (Fleiss' or Krippendorff's alpha), per-skill kappas, and disagreement examples are needed to assess label quality.
evidence: Section 5 reports 90.1% agreement for 62 sampled questions; no kappa or per-skill rates.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flagged inflation risk for skewed labels.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report chance-corrected agreement (Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha) overall and per-skill; provide confusion matrices and illustrative disagreement cases; expand agreement sample if feasible.

concerns.title: Readability measurement circularity via annotator-selected sentences
concerns.description: Computing readability only on sentences selected as necessary couples two annotation steps (sentence selection and skill labeling) and may bias correlations: annotators could preferentially select sentences that highlight difficulty features, altering measured readability relative to whole-context readability.
evidence: Section 3.2 states readability metrics applied only to sentences that need to be read.
Shared analysis recommends recomputing metrics on whole context as a sensitivity check.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report sensitivity analyses: recompute readability metrics on whole contexts and compare correlations; report inter-annotator agreement on sentence selection; test correlations using both selection-based and context-based readability.

concerns.title: Limited statistical reporting for correlation claims
concerns.description: Pearson correlation coefficients are reported (range 0.025–0.416) but p-values, confidence intervals, dataset-stratified statistics, and checks for nonlinear associations or heterogeneity are missing; pooling may mask subgroup effects.
evidence: Section 5 references Table 5 with Pearson r but the paper excerpt lacks p-values/CIs and dataset-stratified diagnostics.
Prior-stage reviewers flagged need for Spearman/nonparametric checks and stratified analyses.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full Table 5 with exact r, p-values, and 95% CIs; compute Spearman rho and report dataset-wise correlations and scatter diagnostics; test for nonlinear relationships or interaction effects.

concerns.title: Sampling representativeness and small per-dataset sample
concerns.description: Sampling 100 questions per dataset (sometimes constrained by development splits or sampling heuristics) may not capture internal heterogeneity; sampling seeds and selection procedures vary across datasets, limiting reproducibility and generalizability.
evidence: Section 4.2 and Appendix A describe different sampling choices (e.g., 1 question per paragraph for SQuAD, filtering NewsQA by metadata).
Shared analysis and other reviewers flagged representativeness concerns.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide sampling code and seeds; present basic diagnostics comparing sampled subset to full dataset on length, topic, and question-type distributions; if feasible, increase sample size for datasets with high internal diversity or demonstrate stability via bootstrap.

concerns.title: Handling and impact of 'nonsense'/'no-answer' items insufficiently analyzed
concerns.description: While annotators could mark 'nonsense' and the authors note prevalence differences across datasets, the paper does not quantify how including/excluding these items affects skill/readability aggregates or correlation analyses.
evidence: Section 5 notes MS MARCO and WDW have higher nonsense rates; NewsQA filtered during selection.
No sensitivity tests reported excluding nonsense items from correlations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report analyses with and without 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' items; quantify their prevalence per dataset and show their effect on mean skill-counts and readability correlations.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct precedent: prior skill taxonomy and multi-perspective analysis of MCTest; paper refines that taxonomy.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper reorganizes and expands Sugawara et al.'s ten skills into 13 with theoretical re-grounding; extends annotation across six datasets rather than two.

comparable_works.relevance: Source of readability features chosen (top 10 features influencing human readability).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Paper reuses top features but applies them to annotator-selected sentences rather than whole texts and acknowledges potential mismatch with system difficulty.

comparable_works.relevance: Provides precedent for dataset sampling sufficiency and highlights dataset quality issues (CNN/Daily Mail errors).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors cite Chen et al. to justify 100-sample choice but do not replicate Chen et al.'s deeper dataset diagnostics.

comparable_works.relevance: Theoretical grounding for decomposing comprehension into strategic comprehension vs text ease.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used as the central theoretical lens to motivate the two metric classes.

uncertainty_flags: Taxonomy overlap: some skills may not be mutually exclusive; operational boundaries need clearer examples and adjudication.
Annotation reliability: percent agreement reported but no chance-corrected statistics or per-skill kappas.
Readability coupling: measuring readability on annotator-selected sentences may confound selection behavior with reading difficulty.
Statistical inference: correlation coefficients lack p-values, CIs, and non-parametric checks; pooled analyses may mask heterogeneity.
Sampling: 100 items/dataset with different sampling heuristics may not be representative of full dataset distributions.
alternative_interpretations: Apparent weak correlation could partly arise from measurement choices: if readability were computed on whole contexts, correlation strengths might change (increase or decrease).
Annotator sentence-selection could systematically omit difficult-to-read but irrelevant sentences, artificially lowering measured readability for hard questions.
High percent agreement might reflect skewed label distributions (many negative labels) rather than reliable positive labeling; per-skill sparsity may inflate agreement.

Dataset regional separation in Figures 3–4 could be driven by genre/collection procedures rather than inherent difficulty axes (e.g., SQuAD's Wikipedia style increases lexical complexity independently of question design).
transparency_notes: Authors describe annotation procedure, dataset sampling, and readability features used; however, key reproducibility artifacts (annotation guidelines, interface screenshots, per-skill label files, sampling seeds/code) should be released or linked.
Inter-annotator agreement should be reported with chance-corrected measures and per-skill statistics to allow external assessment.
Full Table 5 with exact correlation coefficients, p-values, and confidence intervals is necessary for transparent statistical claims.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The two-axis framing (skills × readability) and annotated resource show novelty relative to prior single-dataset or narrower taxonomies; novelty does not ensure validity — methodological checks and validation are required before actionable generalization.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If per-skill labeling demonstrates high chance-corrected agreement and confusion matrices show clear separations, the taxonomy will be robust and useful.
If readability computed on whole contexts yields similar weak correlations, the main empirical claim is strengthened.
If curriculum-style training experiments (easy→hard) using these metric placements improve model learning or transfer, the prescriptive utility claim would be validated.
If sampling expansions confirm dataset-region assignments are stable across larger samples, the comparative dataset claims will generalize.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The 13-skill taxonomy refines previous work and is theoretically motivated; however, lack of formal validation and per-skill reliability reduces confidence that it is a robust incremental advance.
evidence: Section 3.1 taxonomy derivation from Sugawara et al. and cognitive theories.
Absence of per-skill agreement/confusion statistics.
uncertainty_flags: Unclear if new categories (ellipsis, bridging, meta-knowledge) are reliably separable in annotation.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Releasing multi-dataset annotations for skills and sentence-selection is valuable as a resource, enabling follow-up work; its utility depends on annotation transparency and reliability reporting.
evidence: Annotation of 600 questions across six datasets and statements of public release.
Current reporting lacks detailed reliability artifacts required for confident reuse.
uncertainty_flags: Resource usefulness contingent on providing guidelines, per-skill metrics, and sampling code.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Grounded in cognitive theory and intuitively meaningful; empirical application across datasets provides preliminary evidence that axes capture different aspects of difficulty.
evidence: Citations to McNamara & Magliano and Kintsch; Figures showing per-dataset differences.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical separation could be influenced by operational choices (sentence-selection, feature set).

confidence_interval.rationale: Overall confidence in the paper's core contributions is moderate-to-high regarding conceptual framing, annotation effort, and preliminary empirical patterns, but lower regarding quantitative claims about weak correlations and dataset generalizations due to the methodological concerns enumerated (annotation reliability, sampling, measurement coupling, and statistical reporting). The interval reflects combined certainty about strengths and reservations.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a two-axis framing of RC difficulty: prerequisite skills (a refined 13-item taxonomy) and readability (lexical/syntactic/traditional metrics), grounded in cognitive and textual-entailment literature.

The authors operationalized the taxonomy and annotation protocol (three annotators, sentence-selection, multi-label skill assignment) and applied it across six RC datasets (100 sampled questions per dataset), producing a released annotation resource.

Empirical analyses report per-dataset skill-frequency summaries, number-of-skills distributions, readability summaries, and Pearson correlations; visualizations (Figures 3/4) show dataset-specific patterns or clusters in the joint space.

Reviewers agree the central empirical observation is that measured correlations between readability (as operationalized) and number-of-required-skills are weak (reported Pearson r range ~0.025–0.416) and that datasets appear to occupy different regions in the joint metric space.

All reviewers note strengths in theoretical grounding, clear operationalization, cross-dataset application, and the potential utility of a published annotation resource for dataset diagnosis or follow-up work.
disagreements: Degree of novelty/impact: some reviewers view the combined operationalization as a meaningful, novel contribution (integration of taxonomy + readability across multiple datasets), while others judge it as an incremental extension of Sugawara et al. and established readability work.

Severity and centrality of the annotation-reliability concern: all reviewers flag insufficient reporting, but they differ on whether the reported percent-agreement (90.1%) already gives reasonable confidence (some more optimistic) versus it being a critical shortcoming that undermines many quantitative claims (others more critical).

Practical utility claims (curriculum-style ordering): reviewers diverge on how strongly to treat this — some see it as a plausible and actionable direction requiring future validation, others treat it as speculative absent empirical curriculum experiments.

Interpretation of weak correlations: one view treats the weak correlations as evidence that the two axes capture different aspects of difficulty; an alternate view suggests the weak correlations may be an artifact of methodological choices (notably measuring readability only on annotator-selected sentences) and thus require robustness checks before accepting the independence claim.
uncertainty_hotspots: Taxonomy validity & separability: boundaries among several skills (e.g., bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge vs elaboration) are underspecified and lack formal validation (per-skill agreement, confusion matrices, expert adjudication).

Annotation reliability reporting: overall 90.1% is reported without clarification of metric (percent agreement vs chance-corrected), no per-skill kappas or label-wise reliability, and agreement computed on a small subset (62 items) rather than the full annotated set.

Readability measurement dependence: readability metrics were computed only on sentences annotators selected as 'needed' to answer questions; inter-annotator variability in sentence selection is unreported, introducing potential circularity that can bias correlations.

Sampling representativeness: 100 sampled items per dataset with heterogeneous per-dataset sampling heuristics (Appendix A) may not capture dataset heterogeneity; robustness to different samples or stratified sampling is untested.

Statistical analysis completeness: reported Pearson correlation ranges lack p-values, confidence intervals, dataset-stratified coefficients, and non-parametric or non-linear diagnostics (Spearman, mixed-effects, heterogeneity tests).
Treatment of 'nonsense'/'no-answer' items: definitions, annotator instructions, prevalence across full datasets, and sensitivity of analyses to inclusion/exclusion are insufficiently detailed.
model_diversity_effects: Role-driven emphases: structure_analyst and methodology_auditor focused on logical dependencies and reproducibility (highlighting readability–selection circularity and missing robustness checks); novelty assessors emphasized conceptual framing and potential impact but consistently requested validation; claim_verifier concentrated on evidence-vs-assertion distinctions (which claims are well-supported versus which require more reporting).

Because reviewers had differing cognitive roles, criticisms cluster: methodological/process reviewers prioritize reliability, sampling, and statistical rigor; novelty assessors tolerate some methodological gaps if conceptual novelty is present; the divergence underscores that acceptance of the paper's empirical claims depends on both conceptual framing and methodological rigor.

Role-specific effects imply that resolving reliability and robustness concerns would shift consensus toward endorsing the contribution's utility and novelty; conversely, if those concerns persist, the paper's impact will be limited to a preliminary descriptive resource rather than a validated diagnostic framework.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a coherent conceptual framing and a potentially useful annotated resource, but several empirical and reporting gaps limit confidence in the quantitative claims. Editorial decisions should center on whether the manuscript will be revised to address key methodological transparency and robustness items. If a revision is requested, require (at minimum): (1) complete annotation reliability reporting (chance-corrected measures, per-skill kappas, sentence-selection agreement, confusion matrices), (2) sensitivity analyses recomputing readability on whole contexts and on alternative aggregations of selected sentences (union/intersection/random), (3) full statistical reporting for correlation analyses (exact coefficients, p-values, 95% CIs, Spearman/non-parametric checks, dataset-stratified results), (4) sampling reproducibility artifacts (code, seeds, diagnostics comparing sampled subsets to full datasets), and (5) explicit annotation guidelines and example adjudications for ambiguous skill boundaries and for 'nonsense'/'no-answer' decisions. These items are central to evaluating the paper's empirical claims and practical recommendations; the editor should weigh whether the authors can provide these within a reasonable revision timeline.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewer concerns, provide the following evidence and analyses: (1) Annotation reliability: report the exact agreement metric(s) used, compute chance-corrected agreement (Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha) for multi-rater multi-label data, provide per-skill agreement statistics, and include confusion matrices and representative disagreement examples with adjudication notes. Also report inter-annotator overlap statistics for sentence-selection (e.g., average IOU of selected sentence sets). (2) Readability sensitivity: recompute readability metrics on whole contexts and compare correlations with the sentence-selection-based readability; additionally, compute readability on the union and intersection of annotator-selected sentences and report results. (3) Statistical robustness: publish the full correlation table (Table 5) with exact Pearson and Spearman values, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals; run dataset-stratified analyses and consider mixed-effects models with dataset as a random effect and controls (context length, genre). Check for nonlinear relationships (e.g., LOESS/GAM). (4) Sampling transparency: release sampling code and seeds, and provide diagnostics comparing sampled subsets to each full dataset on key covariates (context length, answer type, topic). Consider bootstrap or repeated-sampling stability checks. (5) Taxonomy documentation: include the full annotation manual with decision rubrics and numerous exemplars per skill, and, if possible, a small expert adjudication study or post-hoc co-occurrence/FA/PCA analyses to probe skill separability. (6) 'Nonsense' handling: detail the operational definition, per-dataset prevalence across the full sample, and sensitivity analyses excluding these items from main aggregates. (7) If feasible, provide a short pilot demonstrating whether these axes predict model performance (correlations with baseline system errors) or human difficulty measures; if not feasible, explicitly frame curriculum suggestions as hypotheses for future work. Release the annotation files, instruction text, and analysis scripts alongside the revised manuscript.
transparency_report: Current manuscript provides: (a) taxonomy list and prose definitions (Sec. 3.1), (b) annotation procedure description (Sec. 4.1), (c) sampling heuristics per dataset (Sec. 4.2 and Appendix A), and (d) summary tables/figures (Tables 2–4, Figures 3–4).

Missing or incomplete artifacts flagged by reviewers: (1) annotation guidelines/manual with edge-case examples and the exact instruction text given to annotators, (2) annotation interface screenshots, (3) per-item annotation files (question IDs, per-annotator selected sentence indices, per-annotator multi-label skill vectors), (4) per-skill and sentence-selection agreement statistics and confusion matrices, (5) full correlation table (Table 5) with exact coefficients, p-values and confidence intervals, (6) sampling code and random seeds enabling reproducibility of the 100-item draws, (7) analysis scripts for readability feature computation, and (8) sensitivity/robustness analyses (readability on whole context, alternative correlation metrics).
Reviewers uniformly request that the authors publicly release the annotated dataset and accompanying code to allow independent verification and follow-up analyses.
epistemic_limits: The reviewers' synthesis is constrained by the manuscript excerpt and shared analysis rather than full access to raw annotation files, Table 5 numeric details, and code. Consequently, some judgments (e.g., the practical magnitude of reliability issues or how much robustness checks would alter conclusions) are inferential and conditional. The main empirical claim—that readability and prerequisite-skill metrics are weakly correlated—relies on the particular operationalizations and sampled subsets; without the requested robustness checks and full statistical outputs, the degree to which this finding generalizes to entire datasets, to other readability feature sets, or to model/human difficulty measures remains uncertain. In short, current evidence supports the paper's conceptual framing and descriptive resource value, but quantitative inferences require additional transparency and robustness analyses before they can be treated as well-established.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This manuscript operationalizes reading-comprehension (RC) dataset difficulty along two axes—a refined 13-item prerequisite-skills taxonomy and sentence-level readability features—by collecting multi-label skill annotations and annotator-selected evidence sentences for 100 sampled questions from six RC datasets. The authors report per-dataset skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, readability summaries, and Pearson correlations (reported r range ≈ 0.025–0.416), concluding that readability and prerequisite-skill dimensions capture distinct aspects of difficulty and that datasets occupy different regions in this joint space. An annotation subset is to be released as a resource.
strengths: Conceptually grounded two-axis framing linking cognitive theory (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch) and textual-entailment ideas to operational metrics (skills vs readability).
Concrete operationalization: a 13-skill taxonomy and a reproducible annotation protocol (sentence-selection + multi-label skill tagging) applied across six diverse RC datasets.
Cross-dataset empirical application and intent to publicly release annotated labels, offering a practical resource for dataset diagnosis and follow-up studies.

Descriptive diagnostics (per-skill frequencies, #skills distributions, readability summaries, visualizations) that illuminate dataset construction artifacts (e.g., prevalence of 'nonsense' items in some sources).
limitations: Annotation reliability underreported: inter-annotator agreement is reported as a single percent (90.1% on a 62-item subset) without specification of metric (percent agreement vs chance-corrected) and lacking per-skill kappas, confusion matrices, or sentence-selection overlap statistics; this prevents robust assessment of label quality and may compromise downstream inferences.

Readability measurement dependency: readability features were computed only on sentences annotators selected as 'needed' to answer the question. Because sentence selection and skill labeling were performed jointly, this creates a measurement dependence (possible circularity) that can bias the reported correlation between readability and skill-count and is not accompanied by sensitivity checks (e.g., whole-context readability).

Statistical reporting incomplete: correlation analyses are summarized by ranges (0.025–0.416) but the manuscript does not present full correlation tables with exact coefficients, p-values, confidence intervals, or non-parametric alternatives (Spearman), nor dataset-stratified or mixed-effects analyses to account for heterogeneity.

Sampling and representativeness concerns: 100 sampled questions per dataset (with heterogeneous per-dataset sampling heuristics) may be insufficient to capture internal heterogeneity of large or diverse corpora; sampling code/seeds and diagnostics comparing sampled subsets to full datasets are not provided.
open_questions: Please provide precise annotation-reliability statistics: what agreement metric was used for the reported 90.1%? Provide chance-corrected measures (Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha) overall and per-skill, per-dataset, plus confusion matrices and example disagreement cases.

How do the main correlation results change when readability is computed on whole contexts instead of annotator-selected sentences? Please report correlations (Pearson and Spearman), p-values, and 95% CIs for both operationalizations and for dataset-stratified analyses.

What exact sampling procedure, random seeds, and selection scripts were used for each dataset (Appendix A); can the authors provide diagnostics showing sampled subsets' distributions (context length, question type, genre) vs the full datasets?

How were 'nonsense' and 'no-answer' cases operationally defined and applied? Provide per-dataset prevalence across the full sample, and sensitivity analyses showing results with and without these items included in aggregates/correlations.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree on the conceptual value of framing RC difficulty along two axes (prerequisite skills vs readability) and on the practical value of an annotated multi-dataset resource.

All reviewers identify the manuscript's primary empirical finding as a weak association between readability (as operationalized) and number-of-required-skills, and that sampled datasets appear to occupy distinct regions in the joint space.
There is consensus that the manuscript lacks sufficient reporting on annotation reliability, sampling reproducibility, and statistical robustness to fully support quantitative claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty/impact: some reviewers view the integrated operationalization and cross-dataset annotation as a meaningful, novel contribution; others view it as an incremental extension of prior taxonomies/readability work contingent on stronger validation.

Severity judgment of the single reported agreement statistic: some reviewers consider the 90.1% figure somewhat reassuring despite missing details; others treat the omission of chance-corrected and per-skill agreement as a critical flaw that undermines key analyses.

Practical prescription (curriculum recommendation): some reviewers consider the curriculum suggestion a reasonable hypothesis to explore; others emphasize it is speculative without empirical curriculum experiments linking the axes to learning outcomes.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about taxonomy validity and separability: boundaries between several skills (e.g., bridging vs elaboration; meta-knowledge) are underspecified and lack formal validation (expert adjudication, co-occurrence or factor analyses).

Uncertainty about magnitude and significance of reported correlations: missing p-values/CIs and alternative correlation metrics leave open whether observed coefficients are statistically meaningful or robust to operational choices.

Uncertainty about generalizability: 100-sample-per-dataset draws and heterogeneous sampling heuristics raise questions about whether reported dataset-region placements generalize to full datasets or other RC task formulations.
source_trace: Sugawara et al. (2017) — prior prerequisite-skills taxonomy and small-scale skill annotation; manuscript reports reorganizing their 10 skills into 13 (Sec. 3.1).
Vajjala & Meurers (2012) — source of the readability feature set adopted (top lexical/syntactic features) that the authors apply to annotator-selected sentences (Sec. 3.2).

McNamara & Magliano (2009) and Kintsch (1993) — cognitive-theory grounding for separating strategic comprehension (skills) from text ease (readability) motivating the two-axis framing (Introduction and Sec. 3).
Chen et al. (2016) — precedent for sampling/diagnosing dataset quality (cited to justify 100-sample choice and to highlight dataset noise issues).
transparency_notes: Manuscript provides the 13-skill list, annotation procedure description, dataset sampling heuristics (Appendix A), and summary tables/figures. Missing reproducibility artifacts flagged by reviewers include: (1) the full annotation manual/instruction text and example annotations per skill, (2) per-item annotation files (per-annotator selected sentence indices and multi-label vectors), (3) per-skill and sentence-selection inter-annotator agreement statistics and confusion matrices, (4) full correlation tables (Table 5) with exact coefficients, p-values and 95% CIs, (5) sampling code and random seeds, and (6) scripts used to compute readability features. Reviewers uniformly request these artifacts alongside the released annotations for independent verification.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The manuscript advances a useful conceptual framing and an empirical resource, but quantitative claims require more methodological transparency and robustness tests. If a revision is solicited, request that authors (at minimum) add: (1) chance-corrected annotation reliability (Fleiss' kappa/Krippendorff's alpha) overall and per-skill, sentence-selection overlap statistics, and confusion matrices; (2) sensitivity analyses recomputing readability on whole contexts and on alternative sentence-aggregation strategies (union/intersection) with corresponding correlations (Pearson and Spearman) and p-values/CIs; (3) full correlation reporting (exact Table 5 values, p-values, 95% CIs) and dataset-stratified diagnostics or mixed-effects models controlling for confounds (context length/genre); (4) sampling code/seeds and diagnostics showing sampled subsets vs full datasets; (5) annotation guidelines and representative adjudicated examples for ambiguous skill boundaries and 'nonsense' labels. These additions address the central empirical uncertainties identified by reviewers and will materially affect the interpretability and reuse of the released resource.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential support and the utility of the released resource, provide the following in a revision or supplement: (1) Full annotation documentation: instruction text, decision rubrics, many per-skill exemplars, and interface screenshots. (2) Reliability reporting: specify the exact metric used for the reported 90.1%, compute and report Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for multi-rater multi-label data overall and per-skill, provide confusion matrices, and report sentence-selection overlap (e.g., average IOU). (3) Readability sensitivity: recompute readability features on whole contexts and on union/intersection of annotator-selected sentences; report Pearson and Spearman correlations with skill-count for each operationalization, with p-values and 95% CIs. (4) Statistical robustness: publish full Table 5 values, run dataset-stratified analyses, and consider mixed-effects regression with dataset as random effect and controls (context length, genre). (5) Sampling transparency: release sampling scripts and seeds and include diagnostics comparing sampled subsets to full datasets along key covariates; report bootstrap or repeated-sample stability checks where feasible. (6) Nonsense/no-answer handling: provide definition, per-dataset prevalence, and sensitivity analyses excluding those items. (7) If possible, include an exploratory link between your metrics and model or human difficulty proxies (e.g., baseline system error rates or human response measures); if not, explicitly frame curriculum recommendations as hypotheses for future work. Finally, release annotated files and analysis code to enable community verification.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: This paper operationalizes RC difficulty along two axes—a refined 13-item prerequisite-skills taxonomy and sentence-level readability features—and applies both to 100-sample annotations across six RC datasets. The authors report descriptive diagnostics and a weak association between readability and skill-count, arguing datasets occupy distinct joint-space regions and presenting an annotation resource.
Strengths: Conceptually well-grounded (cognitive + entailment literature), a concrete annotation protocol and taxonomy, cross-dataset empirical application, and a potentially useful released resource.
Limitations: (1) Annotation reliability is insufficiently reported: the single 90.1% figure lacks metric specification, chance-correction, and per-skill or sentence-selection agreement—this undermines confidence in multi-label analyses. (2) Readability is computed only on annotator-selected sentences, coupling measurement to annotator choice and risking circularity in the readability vs skill-count correlation; no sensitivity checks (e.g., whole-context readability) are provided. Additional limitations include incomplete statistical reporting for correlations (missing p-values/CIs, non-parametric checks) and sampling representativeness (100 items/dataset, varied heuristics) that may limit generalizability.
Open Questions: (1) Provide exact agreement metrics (kappa/alpha), per-skill kappas, confusion matrices, and sentence-selection overlap. (2) How do correlations change if readability is computed on whole contexts? Please report Pearson and Spearman values, p-values, and 95% CIs for both operationalizations and dataset-wise. (3) Share sampling code/seeds and diagnostics comparing sampled subsets to full datasets. (4) Provide operational definitions and prevalence statistics for 'nonsense'/'no-answer' and sensitivity analyses including/excluding those items.
Transparency: Manuscript contains taxonomy, annotation procedure, and sampling heuristics, but key reproducibility artifacts are missing: full annotation manual and examples, per-item annotation files, per-skill reliability stats and confusion matrices, full correlation tables with inferential statistics, sampling code/seeds, and analysis scripts for readability. Release of these items is requested by reviewers to enable verification and reuse.

confidence_interval.rationale: The conceptual framing and annotation effort are clearly present and plausible (supporting the upper range), but missing methodological details (per-skill reliability, full statistical outputs, and robustness checks) create substantive uncertainty about the strength and generalizability of the quantitative claims (supporting the lower bound). If authors provide the requested transparency and robustness analyses, confidence in the empirical conclusions would materially increase.
